newsitem.title: RWANDA: Column of Rwandan refugees halts for night.
newsitem.headline: Column of Rwandan refugees halts for night.

text.p: A column of Rwandan Hutu refugees stretching for miles slowly came to a halt late on Saturday as night fell over Central Africa.
On the Zairean side of the border, the teeming town of Goma filled with the smoke of cooking fires. Thousands of families prepared food and erected green plastic shelters against the rain and cold.

Separated children looked for their parents among the more than 200,000 Hutu refugees estimated by U.N. officials to have already returned east to their homeland in Rwanda after two years in wretched border camps inside Zaire.
Half a million more may also be on the move just west of Goma while several hundred thousand have been scattered further south by a Zairean rebel uprising.
During the day the steady flow swamped the Goma-Gisenyi border post. Aid officials gave up trying to register them, but the border remained open.
Joseph Bideri, Rwanda's presidential spokesman, denied a report from the U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR) that the border was being closed to "control the influx".
Reuters journalists at the main crossing quoted Rwandan officers at the border as saying they had orders to close it at 7 p.m. but the barriers did not come down.
"It's pointless trying to count them. It's endless and we are running out of space every second," said a delegate of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
The exodus from Zaire began on Friday after extremist Hutu militia who had ruthlessly controlled Mugunga and other refugee camps fled under attack by Zairean rebels.
Despite the mass movement the United Nations went ahead and voted to dispatch a multinational humanitarian force to tend to their needs.
The 15-member Security Council on Friday unanimously approved the deployment of a Canadian-led multinational force until March 31 to ensure food and medicine reached refugees.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said the rapidly changing situation of refugees streaming back into Rwanda from Zaire could force a change in plans in the multinational force.
Perry told a news conference the United States would consult with its allies after receiving a report this weekend from a survey team in the area.
Rwanda said the refugee exodus meant the force was obsolete before it was even deployed and the world should send aid instead to help Rwanda settle the newcomers.
"Our position is that the force was coming to create this corridor for the refugees to come home and now they are coming home. So we don't see any need for the force to come," Bideri said.
The fighting in eastern Zaire between rebels and Hutu militia backed by Zairean troops continued.

The sound of heavy machineguns echoed west of Mugunga as the rebels, whose alliance includes many Tutsis, chased the Hutu fighters deeper into Zaire. The rebels control three major towns along eastern Zaire's border -- Goma, Bukavu and Uvira.

The road towards Mugunga camp was still full of people, but less dense than before. Mugunga held some 400,000 refugees early this week but is now empty, but for the hacked corpses of more than 20 women and children and some men.
"The road of death is now a road of hope," said Ray Wilkinson of the UNHCR, adding the returnees were in good shape physically and seemed cheerful.
But he also noted that Goma hospital was treating some cases of cholera.

The French relief group Medecins Sans Frontieres (Doctors Without Borders) said in a statement it suspected there were several cases of cholera among refugees who had been in Mugunga. It appealed to rebels in Goma to allow their aid teams in and to reopen Goma airport for relief flights.

The same mass of humanity crossed the border in chaos and panic in the opposite direction two years ago. Then they were fleeing victorious Tutsi rebels who had put an end to the genocide of hundreds of thousands of Tutsis committed by many of the Hutus under the previous Hutu-led government.
Tens of thousands of Hutus died of cholera in Zaire during that exodus. Many still fear revenge attacks from Tutsis after they return home.
"The people decided to come back because they are tired, hungry and fed up," said Maurice Nsengrenwe, a 31-year-old former seminary student who fled Rwanda in 1994.
